To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

RASs are: (1) more transparent in that the process of assessment is less open and less accessible to the public and service users (2) more equitable in the sense that they produce more consistent results but are less likely to reflect the needs of individual service users and (3) simpler and less discretionary in the sense that there are fewer points at which the assessment can be challenged but they produce more arbitrary results and are less likely to take account of the views of service users.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the introduction of RASs has not been the panacea for all ills that it was hoped to be and that it has not led to the development of a more equitable system of resource allocation for community care service users.
RASs are neither transparent nor equitable, are not simpler and do not lead to more consistent decision-making.
RASs have been introduced to provide an objective means of calculating personal budgets and are not a panacea for the problems of community care provision.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

RASs have the potential to improve the transparency of the community care system and to reduce some of the subjectivity in the process but they are not a panacea for the problems of the community care assessment system.

RASs have been introduced without adequate research into their effectiveness and without adequate consideration of their legal and ethical implications and that the Supreme Court judgment in KM has not clarified the law in this area.

the RAS is a blunt instrument that is being used in a crude way to deliver the Government's policy on personal budgets and that it will not be long before it becomes clear that it is not fit for purpose.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of RASS is not a neutral process and that the way in which they are used will have significant implications for the nature of community care provision and for the way in which social work is carried out.

RASs are not 'objective' and 'transparent' as their proponents claim but instead they are a new and potentially dangerous form of'social work' in which the social worker has no discretion to challenge the RAS calculation.

the RAS approach is not only flawed but is also likely to be a significant barrier to the achievement of the government's stated aim of personalisation and the development of individualised community care services.
